title: Overview: the big ideas
summary: The chapter's key concepts and how its sections fit together.

blocks.md: Welcome to **ML Lifecycle** (Vol I). This overview gives you the chapter's big ideas before the section-by-section lessons. Read the claims once, flip the flashcards, then take the warm-up quiz: it is fine to miss questions here, the lessons that follow fill the gaps.

Engineering organizations often split an ML system into three specialties, with one team curating datasets, another tuning model architectures, and a third provisioning serving hardware. The components those teams own remain coupled. The volume and quality of collected data bound which algorithms are viable, the computational structure of the chosen algorithm dictates what hardware can execute it efficiently, and the memory and bandwidth of the target hardware reshape what preprocessing can run at inference.

Where the Hours Go: Quantifying the ML L

rows: An ML system moves through problem definition, data, training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring, each handing the next a concrete artifact, and because learned behavior changes when the world changes, monitoring evidence must flow back to earlier stages, so deployment starts an operational phase rather than ending the project.

A constraint discovered late forces rework in every upstream artifact that relied on its absence (the 4 GB model against a 500 MB device reservation), so rework is estimated by tracing the revise, retrain, and revalidate chain, and propagation runs both backward and forward.

A request becomes a requirement only when stated as a measurable improvement over a named baseline and decomposed into statistical, physical, and operational constraints bound before development, because a metric that diverges from the goal defeats the system before training starts.

Each stage has an input contract, an output contract, and a quality invariant, and enforcing them at the boundaries turns the feedback loop into an audit that names which upstream stage owns a defect.

Evaluation measures and validation decides: a release needs evidence on latency, subgroup performance, calibration, robustness across sites and time, and operational readiness, recorded in an immutable manifest, and a failed threshold routes the fix to the stage that owns it.
Cycle time bounds how many hypotheses a team can test in a fixed calendar, so iteration velocity buys search breadth rather than guaranteed accuracy, and late discoveries multiply the tax.

Accuracy on a curated test set is not deployment readiness, because field captures differ from curated research images (the Thai screening deployment's ungradable images), so validation must sample the conditions the system will meet.
